newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-TOWNSEND FIT TO LIFT SCOTS.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-TOWNSEND FIT TO LIFT SCOTS.

text.p: Scotland's uncomfortable build- up to the Five Nations championship received a timely boost on Friday when Gregor Townsend was declared fully fit to face Wales at Murrayfield.

Townsend, the home side's key attacking figure, will continue to receive treatment on the lower neck injury he suffered in training this week but team manager Arthur Hastie said he was fully confident he would play.

Coach Richie Dixon admitted, however, the Scottish squad had been deflated by news that hooker Kevin McKenzie will be out until next season after a precautionary scan revealed a slipped disc at the base of his neck.

McKenzie will undergo surgery on Friday and team doctor Jimmy Graham confirmed the popular forward would not be able to take part in any contact sport for at least four months, ruling him out of contention for the Lions tour of South Africa.

"This condition is something which can threaten damage to the spinal cord if you continue to put stress on the neck," said Graham. "It is an operation which takes away a piece of the disc that has been pushed out. It's exactly the same thing as a slipped disc further down the spine except that's it's occurring at the top."

McKenzie's replacement Graham Ellis duly wins his first cap at the age of 31 and could not hide his excitement as Scotland jogged through a public final practice session in front of hundreds of schoolchildren at Linlithgow, some 30 km outside Edinburgh.
"I've been playing since I was nine, so I'm delighted to get my chance," he said.

Captain Rob Wainwright, back after a long injury lay-off and determined to concentrate on the Welsh game rather than discuss the odds on him leading the Lions party, was more concerned with pacifying his Army employers whose attention was drawn to an off-guard remark he made about delaying his service in Bosnia at a press conference this week.

Wainwright, an army doctor, has so far managed to juggle both his military and rugby duties but was forced to reaffirm where his priorities lay. "My primary employer is the Army and if they decide to send me anywhere of course I would be at their beck and call," he said.

The Scottish skipper, also a lover of falconry and fine whisky, has thrown down the gauntlet to a Welsh team who have arrived in Edinburgh, where they have not won since 1985, in particularly confident mood.

"On paper they look very exciting, but they've still got to come up here and prove themselves in the Five Nations and deliver the goods at Murrayfield which is an arena they traditionally haven't enjoyed.
"What we need is a nice home win to get our confidence up before we head off down to England."
